claim: Condensins are genome organisers that shape chromosomes and promote their accurate transmission.
source: Condensins are genome organisers that shape chromosomes and promote their accurate transmission.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about condensin function, supported by the citation context of the manuscript.

claim: Several studies have implicated condensins in gene expression, although any mechanisms have remained enigmatic.
source: Several studies have also implicated condensins in gene expression, although any mechanisms have remained enigmatic.
evidence: This statement references prior research findings through citation and acknowledges gaps in mechanistic understanding.

claim: Condensin plays no direct role in the maintenance of the transcriptome during interphase or mitosis in fission and budding yeasts.
source: In contrast to previous studies, we provide compelling evidence that condensin plays no direct role in the maintenance of the transcriptome, neither during interphase nor during mitosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Changes in gene expression in post-mitotic fission yeast cells from condensin inactivation are largely a consequence of chromosome missegregation during anaphase.
source: We further show that the changes in gene expression in post-mitotic fission yeast cells that result from condensin inactivation are largely a consequence of chromosome missegregation during anaphase, which notably depletes the RNA-exosome from daughter cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data including RNA-seq, microscopy, and genetic experiments.

claim: Chromosome missegregation during anaphase depletes the RNA-exosome from daughter cells.
source: the changes in gene expression in post-mitotic fission yeast cells that result from condensin inactivation are largely a consequence of chromosome missegregation during anaphase, which notably depletes the RNA-exosome from daughter cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced Rrp6 and Dis3 in anucleolate cells.

claim: Preventing karyotype abnormalities in daughter cells restores a normal transcriptome despite condensin inactivation.
source: Crucially, preventing karyotype abnormalities in daughter cells restores a normal transcriptome despite condensin inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data from cdc15-140 cut14-208 double mutant cells.

claim: Chromosome instability, rather than a direct role of condensin in transcription, changes gene expression.
source: Thus, chromosome instability, rather than a direct role of condensin in the transcription process, changes gene expression.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in the study.

claim: SMC complexes are ring-shaped ATPases conserved from bacteria to human.
source: Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes (SMC) complexes are ring-shaped ATPases, conserved from bacteria to human, which shape chromosomes and ensure their accurate transmission during cell divisions (Hirano, 2016; Uhlmann, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Eukaryotes possess three distinct SMC protein complexes: condensins, cohesin, and SMC5/6.
source: Eukaryotes possess three distinct SMC protein complexes, named condensins, cohesin and SMC5/6.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SMC complex classification.

claim: Condensins structure and condense chromosomes.
source: Condensins structure and condense chromosomes, cohesin mediates sister-chromatid cohesion and organises topological domains in the genome during interphase, and SMC5/6 promotes proper DNA replication and repair (Hirano, 2016; Uhlmann, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cohesin mediates sister-chromatid cohesion and organises topological domains in the genome during interphase.
source: Condensins structure and condense chromosomes, cohesin mediates sister-chromatid cohesion and organises topological domains in the genome during interphase, and SMC5/6 promotes proper DNA replication and repair (Hirano, 2016; Uhlmann, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SMC5/6 promotes proper DNA replication and repair.
source: Condensins structure and condense chromosomes, cohesin mediates sister-chromatid cohesion and organises topological domains in the genome during interphase, and SMC5/6 promotes proper DNA replication and repair (Hirano, 2016; Uhlmann, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SMC complexes shape the genome by encircling DNA helixes and extruding loops of DNA.
source: A large body of in vivo and in vitro studies has substantiated the idea that SMC complexes shape the genome and preserve its integrity by encircling DNA helixes and, at least partly, by extruding loops of DNA (Ganji et al., 2018; Gibcus et al., 2018; Hirano, 2016; Uhlmann, 2016; van Ruiten and Rowland, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Cohesin and condensins have been widely implicated in the control of gene expression.
source: Besides organising chromosomes, cohesin and condensins have also been widely implicated in the control of gene expression, raising the idea that the two complexes link gene expression to chromosome architecture (Dowen and Young, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The mechanisms through which condensins impact gene expression have remained largely enigmatic.
source: Yet, while our understanding of gene regulation by cohesin has progressed during the last decade (Merkenschlager and Nora, 2016), the mechanisms through which condensins impact on gene expression have remained largely enigmatic.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Condensins are the key drivers of the assembly of mitotic chromosomes.
source: Condensins have been best characterised as the key drivers of the assembly of mitotic chromosomes (Gibcus et al., 2018; Hirano, 2016; Robellet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The reorganisation of chromatin into compact rod-shaped chromosomes during mitosis is essential for accurate genome transmission during anaphase.
source: The profound reorganisation of chromatin fibres into compact and individualised rod-shaped chromosomes that marks the entry into mitosis is essential for the accurate transmission of the genome during anaphase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitotic chromosome function.

claim: When condensin function is impaired, chromosome arms remain entangled and fail to separate, leading to anaphase chromatin bridges and DNA breakage.
source: When the function of condensins is impaired, chromosome arms remain entangled and hence fail to separate, leading to the formation of sustained anaphase chromatin bridges and DNA breakage during telophase and in post-mitotic cells (Cuylen et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2009; Samoshkin et al., 2012; Sutani et al., 1999; Toselli-Mollereau et al., 2016; Woodward et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Condensins are composed of two ATPases (SMC2Cut14 and SMC4Cut3) that associate with three non-SMC subunits.
source: Like all SMC complexes, condensins are composed of two ATPases, called SMC2Cut14 and SMC4Cut3 (fission yeast names are indicated in superscript), that associate with three non-SMC subunits, which regulate the ATPase activity of the holocomplex and govern its association with DNA (Kschonsak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about condensin structure, supported by citation.

claim: Non-SMC subunits regulate the ATPase activity of condensin and govern its association with DNA.
source: Like all SMC complexes, condensins are composed of two ATPases, called SMC2Cut14 and SMC4Cut3 (fission yeast names are indicated in superscript), that associate with three non-SMC subunits, which regulate the ATPase activity of the holocomplex and govern its association with DNA (Kschonsak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Most eukaryotes possess two condensins (condensin I and II) composed of the same SMC2/SMC4 heterodimer but different non-SMC subunits.
source: Most eukaryotes possess two condensins, called condensin I and II, which are composed of the same SMC2/SMC4 heterodimer but two different sets of non-SMC subunits (Hirano, 2016; Robellet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The dynamics of association of condensin I and II with chromosomes differ.
source: Despite their structural and functional similarities, the dynamics of association of condensin I and II with chromosomes differ (Walther et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Condensin II is nuclear during interphase and enriched on chromosomes from prophase until telophase.
source: Condensin II is nuclear during interphase and enriched on chromosomes from prophase until telophase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about condensin II localization.

claim: Condensin I is mostly cytoplasmic during interphase and associates with chromosomes from prometaphase until telophase.
source: Condensin I, in contrast, is mostly cytoplasmic during interphase and associates with chromosomes from prometaphase until telophase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about condensin I localization.

claim: The Dosage Compensation Complex (DCC) in C. elegans associates with the two X chromosomes in hermaphrodites and halves the expression of X-linked genes.
source: A third condensin variant called the Dosage Compensation Complex (DCC) has been described in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, which associates with the two X chromosomes in hermaphrodite animals and halves the expression of X-linked genes by reducing the occupancy of RNA polymerase II (RNA Pol II) (Kruesi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The DCC halves X-linked gene expression by reducing RNA polymerase II occupancy.
source: A third condensin variant called the Dosage Compensation Complex (DCC) has been described in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, which associates with the two X chromosomes in hermaphrodite animals and halves the expression of X-linked genes by reducing the occupancy of RNA polymerase II (RNA Pol II) (Kruesi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Yeasts possess a unique condensin complex similar to condensin I.
source: Yeasts, in contrast, possess a unique condensin complex, similar in terms of primary sequence to condensin I.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast condensin.

claim: In budding yeast, the silencing of heterochromatic mating type genes is alleviated when condensin is impaired.
source: In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the silencing of heterochromatic mating type genes and the position effect exerted by repetitive ribosomal DNA are both alleviated when condensin is impaired (Bhalla et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In budding yeast, the position effect exerted by repetitive ribosomal DNA is alleviated when condensin is impaired.
source: In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the silencing of heterochromatic mating type genes and the position effect exerted by repetitive ribosomal DNA are both alleviated when condensin is impaired (Bhalla et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In fission yeast, SMC4Cut3 is needed to repress tRNA genes and reporter genes inserted into pericentric DNA repeats.
source: Likewise, in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, the SMC4Cut3 subunit of condensin is needed to repress tRNAs genes as well as reporter genes inserted into the pericentric DNA repeats, which are coated with heterochomatin (He et al., 2016; Iwasaki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Depletion of condensin II in C. elegans is linked to increased expression of at least 250 genes.
source: In C. elegans, depletion of condensin II is linked to an increase in the expression of at least 250 genes, but this effect does not correlate with the occupancy of condensin II on chromosomes (Kranz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The effect of condensin II depletion on gene expression in C. elegans does not correlate with condensin II occupancy on chromosomes.
source: In C. elegans, depletion of condensin II is linked to an increase in the expression of at least 250 genes, but this effect does not correlate with the occupancy of condensin II on chromosomes (Kranz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In Drosophila, condensin I has been implicated in the repression of homeotic genes.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, condensin I has been implicated in the repression of homeotic genes (Lupo et al., 2001), whereas condensin II has been reported to take part in the production of antimicrobial peptides (Longworth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In Drosophila, condensin II has been reported to take part in the production of antimicrobial peptides.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, condensin I has been implicated in the repression of homeotic genes (Lupo et al., 2001), whereas condensin II has been reported to take part in the production of antimicrobial peptides (Longworth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Murine peripheral T cells expressing a mutant CAP-H2 exhibit decreased chromatin compaction and increased expression of the proliferative gene Cis.
source: Murine peripheral T cells that express a mutant version of the condensin II CAP-H2 regulatory subunit, exhibit a decreased compaction of chromatin and an increased expression of the proliferative gene Cis (Rawlings et al., 2011), suggesting a possible mechanistic relationship between condensin-mediated chromosome organisation and gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The CAP-H2 mutation leads to only subtle effects on the transcriptome of precursor thymocytes, which might be caused by chromosomal instability.
source: However, another study reported that the same CAP-H2 mutation led to only subtle effects on the transcriptome of precursor thymocytes, which might be caused by chromosomal instability (Woodward et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research and includes speculation about the cause.

claim: Condensin I was found associated with active promoters during M phase in chicken DT40 cells.
source: Perhaps more consistent with a direct role in gene regulation, condensin I was found associated with active promoters during M phase in chicken DT40 cells, and its depletion prior to mitotic entry coincided with a decreased expression during the subsequent G1 phase of a subset of genes to which it bound to (Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Depletion of condensin I prior to mitotic entry coincided with decreased expression during G1 phase of a subset of genes to which it bound.
source: Perhaps more consistent with a direct role in gene regulation, condensin I was found associated with active promoters during M phase in chicken DT40 cells, and its depletion prior to mitotic entry coincided with a decreased expression during the subsequent G1 phase of a subset of genes to which it bound to (Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Cohesin and condensin II have been detected at super-enhancers in rapidly proliferating mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: Similarly, cohesin and condensin II have been detected at super-enhancers in rapidly proliferating mouse embryonic stem cells, and depleting condensin II has been associated with a reduced expression of cell-identity genes driven by these super-enhancers (Dowen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Depleting condensin II has been associated with reduced expression of cell-identity genes driven by super-enhancers.
source: Similarly, cohesin and condensin II have been detected at super-enhancers in rapidly proliferating mouse embryonic stem cells, and depleting condensin II has been associated with a reduced expression of cell-identity genes driven by these super-enhancers (Dowen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Condensin II depletion affects expression of highly-expressed housekeeping genes in mouse embryonic stem cells and human embryonic kidney cells.
source: Yuen et al. observed a similar effect on the expression of highly-expressed housekeeping genes in mouse embryonic stem cells and human embryonic kidney cells (Yuen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Condensin I and II bind enhancers activated by β-estradiol during interphase in human MCF7 cells.
source: Finally, it has been reported that not only condensin II, but also condensin I, binds enhancers activated by β-estradiol during interphase in human MCF7 breast adenocarcinoma cells, and that the depletion of condensin I or II led to a reduced transcription of oestrogen-activated genes (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Depletion of condensin I or II led to reduced transcription of oestrogen-activated genes in MCF7 cells.
source: Finally, it has been reported that not only condensin II, but also condensin I, binds enhancers activated by β-estradiol during interphase in human MCF7 breast adenocarcinoma cells, and that the depletion of condensin I or II led to a reduced transcription of oestrogen-activated genes (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The same enhancers occupied by condensin I and II in MCF7 cells were also occupied by cohesin and rely upon cohesin to drive gene expression.
source: Intriguingly, the same enhancers where also found occupied by cohesin and to rely upon this complex to drive gene expression (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Mitotic chromosomes conserve considerable chromatin accessibility similar to interphase chromatin.
source: Mitotic chromosomes conserve considerable chromatin accessibility, similar to interphase chromatin (Hihara et al., 2012), and DNA remains accessible to transcription factors even in mitotic chromosomes that have been structured by condensin complexes (Chen et al., 2005; Palozola et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: DNA remains accessible to transcription factors in mitotic chromosomes structured by condensin complexes.
source: Mitotic chromosomes conserve considerable chromatin accessibility, similar to interphase chromatin (Hihara et al., 2012), and DNA remains accessible to transcription factors even in mitotic chromosomes that have been structured by condensin complexes (Chen et al., 2005; Palozola et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The loss or gain of chromosomes is sufficient to alter gene expression.
source: Furthermore, given that the loss or gain of chromosomes is sufficient to alter gene expression (Santaguida and Amon, 2015; Sheltzer et al., 2012), it is crucial to determine to which extent the role attributed to condensin I and II in the control of gene expression is mechanistically different from, or related to, the assembly and segregation of chromosomes during mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gene expression can be controlled at the transcriptional level by changing RNA polymerase activity and/or occupancy.
source: Gene expression can be controlled at the transcriptional level by changing the activity and/or the occupancy of RNA polymerases, as exemplified by condensinDCC (Kruesi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citation to an example.

claim: Gene expression can be controlled at the co- or post-transcriptional level by modulating transcript half-life.
source: It can also be controlled at the co- or post-transcriptional level by modulating the half-life of transcripts (Bühler et al., 2007; Harigaya et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The RNA-exosome is a conserved ribonuclease complex that ensures maturation and controlled degradation of RNAs.
source: The RNA-exosome is a conserved ribonuclease complex that ensures the maturation and the controlled degradation of a plethora of RNAs in the cell, including, for example, defective RNAs or cryptic unstable non-coding RNAs (Kilchert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The RNA-exosome consists of nine core subunits that associate with RNase Dis3 in the cytoplasm and RNase Rrp6 in the nucleus.
source: The RNA-exosome consists of nine core subunits that associate with the RNase Dis3 in the cytoplasm, plus a second RNase, called Rrp6, in the nucleus (Kilchert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Cofactors such as the TRAMP complex stimulate RNA-exosome RNase activity and specify its targets.
source: Cofactors, such as the TRAMP poly(A)polymerase complex, stimulate the RNase activity of the RNA-exosome and specify its targets (Kilchert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Rrp6 has been found associated with chromosomes at actively transcribed genes.
source: Rrp6 has been found associated with chromosomes at actively transcribed genes (Andrulis et al., 2002), leading to the idea that the RNA-exosome can handle nuclear RNA in a co-transcriptional manner.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The RNA-exosome can handle nuclear RNA in a co-transcriptional manner.
source: Rrp6 has been found associated with chromosomes at actively transcribed genes (Andrulis et al., 2002), leading to the idea that the RNA-exosome can handle nuclear RNA in a co-transcriptional manner.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from prior research findings.

claim: The RNA-exosome plays a central role in proper gene expression by processing and eliminating cellular transcripts.
source: By processing and eliminating cellular transcripts, the RNA-exosome plays a central role in proper gene expression (Kilchert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: 306 transcripts were differentially expressed in the cut14-208 condensin mutant compared to wild type.
source: We identified 306 transcripts that were differentially expressed with log2 fold changes superior to 0.5 or inferior to −0.5 (FDR ≤ 0.05) in the cut14-208 condensin mutant compared to wild type (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 98.5% of differentially expressed transcripts in cut14-208 exhibited increased steady-state levels.
source: The vast majority of transcripts (98.5%; n = 302/306) exhibited an increased steady-state level in the mutant.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Gene expression is altered and mainly increased in dividing condensin mutant cut14-208 cells.
source: Thus, gene expression is altered, and mainly increased, in dividing condensin mutant cut14-208 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data.

claim: 57% of misregulated transcripts in cut14-208 were mRNAs and 43% were non-coding RNAs.
source: Of the 306 misregulated transcripts, 57% were mRNAs and the remaining 43% were non-protein coding RNAs (ncRNA) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Histone mRNAs were found amongst the upregulated transcripts in cut14-208, confirming previous observations.
source: We found histone mRNAs amongst the upregulated transcripts, confirming previous observations (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This finding from the current study confirms prior research cited.

claim: Analysis of all increased mRNAs revealed no enrichment for a specific gene ontology term.
source: However, the analysis of all increased mRNAs revealed no enrichment for a specific gene ontology (GO) term, which suggests that condensin inactivation does not affect the expression of a particular family of protein-coding genes.
evidence: This is a finding from GO term analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Condensin inactivation does not affect the expression of a particular family of protein-coding genes.
source: However, the analysis of all increased mRNAs revealed no enrichment for a specific gene ontology (GO) term, which suggests that condensin inactivation does not affect the expression of a particular family of protein-coding genes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from GO term analysis.

claim: ncRNAs were significantly enriched in the population of transcripts up-regulated in the cut14-208 mutant.
source: In contrast, ncRNAs, which represent ~22% of the transcription units in the fission yeast genome (n = 1524/6986; genome version ASM294v2.30), were significantly enriched in the population of transcripts up-regulated in the cut14-208 mutant (p<0.001, Chi-square test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: ncRNAs represent approximately 22% of transcription units in the fission yeast genome.
source: In contrast, ncRNAs, which represent ~22% of the transcription units in the fission yeast genome (n = 1524/6986; genome version ASM294v2.30), were significantly enriched in the population of transcripts up-regulated in the cut14-208 mutant (p<0.001, Chi-square test).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about genome annotation.

claim: Most ncRNAs are maintained at a low level by the nuclear RNA-exosome.
source: Since most ncRNAs are maintained at a low level by the nuclear RNA-exosome (Wilhelm et al., 2008), their controlled degradation might be compromised in the mutant.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The antisense ncRNA mug93as accumulated in cells lacking Rrp6 or defective for Dis3.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, mug93as was barely detectable in a wild-type background but accumulated in cells lacking Rrp6 or defective for Dis3, as expected if it were degraded by the RNA-exosome.
evidence: This is a finding from northern blot analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: mug93as accumulated in cut14-208 mutant cells to levels reminiscent of the rrp6Δ control.
source: Remarkably, mug93as also accumulated in cut14-208 mutant cells, reaching levels reminiscent of the rrp6Δ control.
evidence: This is a finding from northern blot analysis.

claim: ChIP against RNA Pol II revealed no change in RNA Pol II occupancy at mug93as, ncRNA.489, or ncRNA.540 genes in cut14-208 cells.
source: Furthermore, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) against RNA Pol II revealed no change in RNA Pol II occupancy at neither the mug93as gene, nor two additional example ncRNA genes (ncRNA.489 and ncRNA.540), in cut14-208 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), although their ncRNA levels were increased between 5- and 30-fold (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ncRNA levels were increased between 5- and 30-fold in cut14-208 cells despite no change in RNA Pol II occupancy.
source: Furthermore, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) against RNA Pol II revealed no change in RNA Pol II occupancy at neither the mug93as gene, nor two additional example ncRNA genes (ncRNA.489 and ncRNA.540), in cut14-208 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), although their ncRNA levels were increased between 5- and 30-fold (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR and ChIP data.

claim: Increased ncRNAs in cut14-208 cells might accumulate due to impaired degradation rather than increased transcription.
source: These RNAs might therefore accumulate due to impaired degradation rather than increased transcription.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combination of RNA-seq and ChIP data.

claim: Unstable RNA species accumulate when condensin is defective.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that unstable RNA species accumulate when condensin is defective.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings.

claim: 663 RNAs were differentially expressed in the rrp6Δ mutant.
source: We identified 663 RNAs that were differentially expressed with log2 fold changes superior to 0.5 or inferior to −0.5 (FDR ≤ 0.05) in the rrp6Δ mutant (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 78% of differentially expressed RNAs in rrp6Δ were increased in levels and 22% were decreased.
source: Of these differentially expressed RNAs, 78% were increased in levels and 22% were decreased.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The population of Rrp6-sensitive RNAs was considerably enriched in ncRNAs.
source: The population of Rrp6-sensitive RNAs was considerably enriched in ncRNAs (p<0.001, Chi-square test) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Approximately 43% of RNAs that accumulated in cut14-208 also accumulated in rrp6Δ cells.
source: Pairwise comparison with cut14-208 revealed that ~ 43% (n = 129/302) of the RNAs that accumulated in the condensin mutant also accumulated in cells lacking Rrp6 (Figure 1G,H), with no clear preference for ncRNA and mRNA transcripts (50% each).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparative RNA-seq analysis shown in Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: The overlap between RNAs accumulated in cut14-208 and rrp6Δ was statistically highly significant.
source: A hypergeometric test confirmed that this overlap was statistically highly significant (p=4.6e−55).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from hypergeometric test analysis.

claim: A large fraction of transcripts that accumulate when condensin is impaired are normally targeted by the ribonuclease Rrp6.
source: These data indicate that a large fraction of the transcripts that accumulate when condensin is impaired are normally targeted by the ribonuclease Rrp6.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overlap analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Visual inspection of RNA-seq profile of cut14-208 revealed widespread increase of reads downstream of 3' ends of genes.
source: Visual inspection of the RNA-seq profile of the cut14-208 mutant revealed a widespread increase of reads downstream of the 3' ends of genes, suggesting defects in the termination of transcription (for an example, see the hsp9 gene in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from RNA-seq data visualization shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Dis3 and Rrp6 prevent the accumulation of read-through transcripts.
source: Dis3 and Rrp6 have been reported to prevent the accumulation of read-through transcripts, although through possibly different mechanisms (Lemay et al., 2014; Zofall et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: 3'-extended hsp9 RNAs accumulate in fission yeast cells when Dis3 is impaired, and to a lesser extent when Rrp6 is lacking.
source: Lemay et al. have shown that 3'-extended hsp9 RNAs accumulate in fission yeast cells when Dis3 is impaired, and to a lesser extent when Rrp6 is lacking (Lemay et al., 2014).
evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claim: cut14-208 mutant cells accumulated 3'-extended hsp9 RNA of the same length as cells depleted of Dis3 or Rrp6.
source: Importantly, cut14-208 mutant cells accumulated 3'-extended hsp9 RNA of the same length as cells depleted of Dis3 or Rrp6.
evidence: This is a finding from northern blot analysis.

claim: Other condensin mutants (cut3-477 and cut14-180) also accumulated read-through hsp9 RNA.
source: Moreover, other condensin mutants, such as cut3-477 and cut14-180, also accumulated read-through hsp9 RNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which demonstrates that the accumulation of uncleaved, 3'-extended hsp9 transcripts is a feature of condensin inactivation.
evidence: This is a finding from northern blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The accumulation of uncleaved, 3'-extended hsp9 transcripts is a feature of condensin inactivation.
source: Moreover, other condensin mutants, such as cut3-477 and cut14-180, also accumulated read-through hsp9 RNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which demonstrates that the accumulation of uncleaved, 3'-extended hsp9 transcripts is a feature of condensin inactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data across multiple condensin mutants.

claim: 489 transcripts were extended at their 3' ends in cut14-208 cells, mostly mRNAs and ncRNAs.
source: Using these criteria, we identified 489 transcripts, mostly mRNAs and ncRNAs, which were extended at their 3' ends (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from systematic RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Read-through RNAs were polyadenylated.
source: Oligo(dT)-primed RT-PCR showed that read-through RNAs were polyadenylated (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from oligo(dT)-primed RT-PCR shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GO term analysis revealed no specific feature defining the population of read-through transcripts in cut14-208 cells.
source: GO term analysis revealed no specific feature defining the population of read-through transcripts that accumulate in cut14-208 cells.
evidence: This is a finding from GO term analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Only 111 of the 489 read-through transcripts were also up-regulated.
source: Furthermore, only 111 of the 489 read-through transcripts were also up-regulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), which suggests that the 3'-extended RNAs were not the by-product of increased transcription.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The 3'-extended RNAs were not the by-product of increased transcription.
source: Furthermore, only 111 of the 489 read-through transcripts were also up-regulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), which suggests that the 3'-extended RNAs were not the by-product of increased transcription.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overlap analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: ChIP against transcriptionally active RNA Pol II revealed no increased occupancy downstream canonical TTS in cut14-208 mutant cells.
source: In addition, ChIP against transcriptionally active RNA Pol II revealed no increased occupancy downstream canonical TTS in cut14-208 mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), in contrast to the transcription termination mutant pfs2-11 that we used as control (Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The termination of transcription remains largely effective in cut14-208 mutant cells.
source: This result suggests that the termination of transcription remains largely effective in cut14-208 mutant cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from ChIP data.

claim: 3'-extended transcripts in cut14-208 cells are unlikely to stem from increased transcription beyond the TTS.
source: The 3'-extended transcripts that accumulate in cut14-208 cells are, therefore, unlikely to stem from an increased transcription beyond the TTS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from ChIP and RNA-seq data.

claim: Condensin and cohesin frequently, but not systematically, co-localise along chromosomes.
source: Condensin and cohesin frequently, but not systematically, co-localise along chromosomes (Kim et al., 2016; Nakazawa et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The accumulation of cohesin at the 3' ends of co-transcribed convergent genes locally strengthens the termination of transcription.
source: It has been proposed that the accumulation of cohesin at the 3' ends of co-transcribed convergent genes locally strengthens the termination of transcription (Gullerova and Proudfoot, 2008).
evidence: This is a prior hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: There is an enrichment for genes in a convergent orientation throughout the fission yeast genome (~62%).
source: As previously observed (Schmidt et al., 2009), we found an enrichment for genes in a convergent orientation throughout the fission yeast genome (~62%, n = 4302/6986).
evidence: This is a finding from genome annotation analysis, confirming prior observations.

claim: Read-through transcripts in cut14-208 emanated mostly from genes oriented in tandem (53%) and slightly less from convergent genes (47%).
source: In contrast, the read-through transcripts that accumulated in the cut14-208 mutant emanated mostly from genes oriented in tandem (53%, n = 259/489) and slightly less from convergent genes (47%, n = 230/489).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: No change in the localisation of cohesin was observed at genes with read-through transcripts or at up-regulated genes in cut14-208 mutant cells.
source: We also analysed the localisation of cohesin in cut14-208 cells grown at the restrictive temperature, using ChIP against the SMC3Psm3 subunit of cohesin tagged with GFP. We observed no change in the localisation of Psm3-GFP neither at genes with read-through transcripts nor at up-regulated genes in cut14-28 mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: No read-through RNAs were observed at nmt2, tea3, mei4, or pdt1 genes in cut14-208 background.
source: Read-through transcripts have been detected at the nmt2, tea3, mei4 and pdt1 genes in cohesin mutant cells (Gullerova and Proudfoot, 2008). In sharp contrast, we observed no read-through RNAs at any of these four genes in a cut14-208 background (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, contrasting with prior research.

claim: Cohesin binding to chromatin and cohesin-dependent transcription termination remain largely unaffected when condensin is impaired by cut14-208.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that both cohesin binding to chromatin and cohesin-dependent transcription termination remain largely unaffected when condensin is impaired by the cut14-208 mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from ChIP and RNA-seq data.

claim: 622 read-through RNAs, mostly mRNAs and ncRNAs, were detected in rrp6Δ cells.
source: We detected 622 read-through RNAs, again mostly mRNAs and ncRNAs, in the transcriptome of cells lacking Rrp6 (Figure 2E), which confirms previous reports (Lemay et al., 2014; Zofall et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2E, confirming prior research.

claim: Pol II occupancy remained unchanged downstream the TTS of genes with read-through transcripts in rrp6Δ cells.
source: Pol II occupancy remained unchanged downstream the TTS of genes with read-through transcripts in rrp6Δ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), consistent with the idea that Rrp6 is needed to eliminate read-though RNAs at the co- or post-transcriptional level (Zofall et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, consistent with prior research.

claim: 50% of read-through RNAs that accumulated in rrp6Δ cells were also extended at their 3' ends in cut14-208 mutant.
source: Importantly, 50% of the read-through RNAs that accumulated in cells lacking Rrp6 were also extended at their 3'ends in the cut14-208 mutant (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparative RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The function of Rrp6 might be affected in a cut14-208 background.
source: This reinforces the idea that the function of Rrp6 might be affected in a cut14-208 background.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overlap of read-through transcripts.

claim: The steady state level of the Rrp6 protein remained unchanged in cut14-208 mutant cells.
source: The steady state level of the Rrp6 protein remained unchanged in cut14-208 mutant cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: No change was observed in the mRNA levels of RNA-exosome or TRAMP components in cut14-208 mutant by RNA-seq.
source: Likewise, we observed no change by RNA-seq in the mRNA levels of RNA-exosome or TRAMP components in the condensin mutant (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 3'-extended read-through transcripts accumulate upon condensin inactivation in fission yeast.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that 3'-extended read-through transcripts accumulate upon condensin inactivation in fission yeast and that this accumulation might stem from defects in the processing of these transcripts by Rrp6.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings.

claim: The accumulation of read-through transcripts might stem from defects in their processing by Rrp6.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that 3'-extended read-through transcripts accumulate upon condensin inactivation in fission yeast and that this accumulation might stem from defects in the processing of these transcripts by Rrp6.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the data.

claim: cdc10-129 single mutant and cdc10-129 cut14-208 double mutant cells completed S phase and progressed through G2 phase and mitosis with similar kinetics.
source: FACScan analysis of DNA content and cytological observations revealed that cdc10-129 single mutant and cdc10-129 cut14-208 double mutant cells completed S phase (t = 30 min after release) and progressed through G2 phase (t = 60 min) and mitosis (t = 90 min) with similar kinetics (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from FACScan and cytological analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Chromosome segregation was impaired in the cut14-208 mutant background, as revealed by anaphase chromatin bridges.
source: Chromosome segregation was impaired in the cut14-208 mutant background, as revealed by the appearance of anaphase chromatin bridges (Figure 3B, green line), which were subsequently severed by the septum upon mitotic exit, producing the CUT phenotype (Cells Untimely Torn) (Figure 3B, red line).
evidence: This is a finding from cytological analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FACScan analysis revealed the appearance of aberrant karyotypes in post-mitotic cut14-208 cells.
source: Accordingly, FACScan analysis revealed the appearance of aberrant karyotypes in post-mitotic cells (t = 120 and 180 min; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from FACScan analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No up-regulation of reporter RNAs was detected during G2 phase in synchronized cdc10-129 cut14-208 cells.
source: Remarkably, we detected no up-regulation of any of the three reporter RNAs that we had selected from the pool of upregulated transcripts in cut14-208 mutants (Figure 1B) during G2 phase in synchronized cdc10-129 cut14-208 cells (t = 60 min, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Reporter RNAs started to accumulate at t = 90 min and further increased at t = 120 min and 180 min, coinciding with accumulation of aneuploid post-mitotic cells.
source: These RNAs started to accumulate, however, at t = 90 min and further increased at t = 120 min and 180 min (Figure 3C), coincidently with the accumulation of aneuploid post-mitotic cells.
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3C, correlated with FACScan data.

claim: Condensin is possibly required for proper gene expression during late mitosis or early G1 phase.
source: This result suggests that condensin is possibly required for proper gene expression during late mitosis or early G1 phase.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the timing of RNA accumulation.

claim: No up-regulation of reporter RNAs was observed at any time point when cut14-208 cells were arrested at G2/M transition.
source: To validate these results, we repeated the RT-qPCR measurements by synchronously releasing cut14-208 cells from the early S phase block only 1 hr after shifting the temperature to 36°C and re-arrested them already at the G2/M transition using a cdc25-22 mutation (Figure 3D,E). In this time course experiment, we observed no up-regulation of the reporter RNAs at any time point (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: RNA levels remained unchanged after a sustained arrest in metaphase by depletion of Slp1.
source: Similarly, RNA levels remained unchanged after a sustained arrest in metaphase at 36°C by depletion of the anaphase promoting complex (APC/C) activator Slp1 (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figures 3G-I.

claim: In fission yeast, the function of condensin is dispensable for gene regulation during S and G2 phases of the cell cycle.
source: We conclude that, in fission yeast, the function of condensin is dispensable for gene regulation during S and G2 phases of the cell cycle, consistent with the finding that condensin is largely displaced from the nucleus during this time (Sutani et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple synchronization experiments, consistent with prior research.

claim: Condensin in budding yeast remains bound to chromosomes throughout the cell cycle.
source: Condensin in the budding yeast S. cerevisiae remains, in contrast, bound to chromosomes throughout the cell cycle (D'Ambrosio et al., 2008b), which is reminiscent to the continuous nuclear localization of the condensin II complex in metazoan cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Condensin localizes to chromosomes of budding yeast cells released synchronously from G1 arrest.
source: We first confirmed that condensin localizes to chromosomes of cells released synchronously into the cell cycle from a G1 mating pheromone arrest (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from chromosome spreading and ChIP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Condensin bound to chromosomes during G1 phase in budding yeast and its levels increased as cells passed through S and G2 phases.
source: Chromosome spreading and ChIP showed that condensin bound to chromosomes already during G1 phase and that its levels on chromosomes increased as cells passed through S and G2 phases (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from chromosome spreading and ChIP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: TEV cleavage of the Brn1 subunit efficiently released condensin from chromosomes in budding yeast.
source: To inactivate condensin in budding yeast, we proteolytically cleaved the kleisin (Brn1) subunit of the condensin ring by inducing expression of a site-specific protease from tobacco etch virus (TEV) using a galactose-inducible promoter, which efficiently released condensin from chromosomes (Cuylen et al., 2011), even during G1 phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, using a method from prior research.

claim: Only 26 transcripts were differentially expressed by at least two-fold in G1 phase-arrested budding yeast cells after condensin cleavage.
source: We then compared the transcriptome of G1 phase-arrested cells after condensin cleavage to cells with intact condensin (Figure 4A). Remarkably, solely 26 transcripts were differentially expressed by at least two-fold (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from tiling array analysis shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Only six genes displayed an up- or downregulation of two-fold or more when budding yeast cells were released from G1 arrest after Brn1 cleavage and re-arrested in M phase.
source: To rule out that such minor effect on gene expression was not an artefact caused by the G1 phase arrest, we repeated the experiment, but this time released cells after Brn1 TEV cleavage from the G1 phase arrest and re-arrested them in the subsequent M phase by addition of the spindle poison nocodazole, before preparing RNA for transcriptome analysis (Figure 4C). In this experiment, only six genes displayed an up- or downregulation of two-fold or more (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from tiling array analysis shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Condensin inactivation by releasing the complex from chromosomes has no major effects on gene expression in budding yeast cells prevented from undergoing division.
source: We conclude that condensin inactivation by releasing the complex from chromosomes has no major effects on the gene expression program of budding yeast cells when these cells are prevented from undergoing division.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from tiling array experiments in budding yeast.

claim: Defects in chromosome segregation caused by condensin inactivation might be causally responsible for condensin-dependent gene deregulation.
source: The fact that we observed changes in transcript levels in asynchronously dividing cut14-208 fission yeast mutant cells, but not in fission or budding yeast condensin mutants that are prevented from undergoing anaphase, raises the possibility that defects in chromosome segregation caused by condensin inactivation might be causally responsible for condensin-dependent gene deregulation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from comparing results across different experimental conditions.

claim: An increase in transcript levels was measured after mitotic exit and chromosome severing when cut14-208 cells were arrested at G2/M transition and then released.
source: Indeed, when we arrested fission yeast cut14-208 cells at the G2/M transition using the analogue-sensitive Cdc2asM17 kinase (Aoi et al., 2014), shifted the temperature to 36°C and then released them from the arrest to complete mitosis, we measured an increase in transcript levels after mitotic exit and the severing of chromosomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Mutation of separase (ptr4-1) or APC/C (cut9-665) resulted in chromosome missegregation and severing, as well as increased RNA levels.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, mutation of separase (ptr4-1) or of a subunit of the APC/C (cut9-665) resulted in chromosome missegregation and severing by the cytokinetic ring upon mitotic exit, as well as an increase in RNA levels, in a manner similar to cut14-208.
evidence: This is a finding from cytological analysis and RT-qPCR shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The amplitude of increase in RNA levels correlated with the frequency of chromosome cutting in different mutants.
source: Moreover, the amplitude of the increase in RNA levels correlated with the frequency of chromosome cutting in the different mutants (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis of cytological and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Analysis of five additional condensin mutations confirmed the correlation between RNA increase and chromosome missegregation prevalence.
source: The analysis of five additional condensin mutations of increasing prevalence of chromosome missegregation further confirmed this correlation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of multiple condensin mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Double mutant cdc15-140 cut14-208 cells exhibited chromatin bridges during anaphase at 36°C.
source: Double mutant cells cdc15-140 cut14-208 exhibited chromatin bridges during anaphase at 36°C (Figure 5B), which indicates that cdc15-140 did not suppress the chromosome segregation defect caused by the cut14-208 mutation.
evidence: This is a finding from cytological analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: cdc15-140 did not suppress the chromosome segregation defect caused by cut14-208.
source: Double mutant cells cdc15-140 cut14-208 exhibited chromatin bridges during anaphase at 36°C (Figure 5B), which indicates that cdc15-140 did not suppress the chromosome segregation defect caused by the cut14-208 mutation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cytological observations.

claim: Chromatin bridges were no longer severed upon mitotic exit in cdc15-140 cut14-208 double mutant cells.
source: However, in the absence of a cytokinetic ring, these chromatin bridges were no longer severed upon mitotic exit.
evidence: This is a finding from cytological analysis.

claim: The gain or loss of chromosomal fragments and production of post-mitotic cells with unbalanced karyotypes were suppressed when cytokinesis was prevented.
source: As a consequence, the gain or loss of chromosomal fragments and the production of post-mitotic cells with unbalanced karyotypes were suppressed when cytokinesis was prevented (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from FACScan analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Approximately 98% of RNAs up-regulated in cut14-208 single mutant were no longer detected as differentially expressed in cut14-208 cdc15-140 double mutant.
source: Remarkably, parallel RNA-seq analysis revealed that ~98% of the RNAs up-regulated in the cut14-208 single mutant were no-longer detected as differentially expressed in the cut14-208 cdc15-140 double mutant (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: The production of read-through transcripts was suppressed by cdc15-140.
source: The production of read-through transcripts was similarly suppressed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: RNA levels remained increased in the cdc15-140 rrp6Δ mutant.
source: Note that RNA levels remained increased in the cdc15-140 rrp6Δ mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), ruling out a potential compensatory effect of cdc15-140 on Rrp6 deficiency per se.
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: cdc12-112 mutation equally restored normal gene expression in the cut14-208 genetic background.
source: Finally, we found that cdc12-112, another mutation that also impairs cytokinesis (Chang et al., 1997), equally restored normal gene expression in the cut14-208 genetic background (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), which confirms that cytokinesis was a driving force for the gene deregulation exhibited by the cut14-208 mutant.
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D, confirming the role of cytokinesis.

claim: Cytokinesis is a driving force for gene deregulation exhibited by the cut14-208 mutant.
source: Finally, we found that cdc12-112, another mutation that also impairs cytokinesis (Chang et al., 1997), equally restored normal gene expression in the cut14-208 genetic background (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), which confirms that cytokinesis was a driving force for the gene deregulation exhibited by the cut14-208 mutant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with multiple cytokinesis mutants.

claim: Changes in mRNA and ncRNA levels in cut14-208 cells are mostly, if not entirely, the consequence of chromosome cleavage during cytokinesis.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that changes in mRNA and ncRNA levels exhibited by cut14-208 condensin mutant cells are mostly, if not entirely, the consequence of chromosome cleavage during cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments with cytokinesis mutants.

claim: The severing of chromosomes by the cytokinetic ring leads to DNA damage and formation of genomically unbalanced daughter cells.
source: The severing of chromosomes by the cytokinetic ring leads not only to DNA damage, as revealed by the accumulation of sustained Rad22-GFP foci (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), but also to the formation of genomically unbalanced daughter cells, as shown by FACScan analysis of DNA contents (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy and FACScan analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3B.

claim: Both DNA damage and genomic imbalance phenotypes coincide with the increase in RNA levels and are suppressed by cdc15-140.
source: Both phenotypes coincide with the increase in RNA levels, and both are suppressed by cdc15-140 (Figure 5B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from multiple analyses shown in Figure 5B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DNA damage induced by Camptothecin or Zeocin did not increase ncRNA or mRNA levels.
source: The appearance of sustained Rad22-GFP foci in cells treated with Camptothecin or Zeocin confirmed the accumulation of DNA damage (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). However, RT-qPCR revealed no increase in ncRNA or mRNA levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), arguing that DNA damage is not the main driver for gene deregulation in cut14-208 mutant cells.
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy and RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DNA damage is not the main driver for gene deregulation in cut14-208 mutant cells.
source: The appearance of sustained Rad22-GFP foci in cells treated with Camptothecin or Zeocin confirmed the accumulation of DNA damage (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). However, RT-qPCR revealed no increase in ncRNA or mRNA levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), arguing that DNA damage is not the main driver for gene deregulation in cut14-208 mutant cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from DNA damage experiments.

claim: The mis6-302 mutation disrupts kinetochore assembly and leads to production of aneuploid post-mitotic cells.
source: To test the impact of genomic imbalance on gene expression, we used the thermosensitive mis6-302 mutation which disrupts kinetochore assembly, and hence accurate chromosome segregation during anaphase, leading to the production of aneuploid post-mitotic cells (Saitoh et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mis6-302 mutation supported by citation.

claim: mis6-302 causes neither chromatin bridges nor a CUT phenotype.
source: Note that mis6-302 causes neither chromatin bridges nor a CUT phenotype.
evidence: This is an observation about the phenotype of mis6-302.

claim: FACScan analysis of mis6-302 cells confirmed the appearance of genomically unbalanced cells.
source: FACScan analysis of mis6-302 cells grown at the restrictive temperature confirmed the appearance of genomically unbalanced cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a finding from FACScan analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: RT-qPCR of four reporter RNAs revealed a similar increase in mis6-302 cells as in cut14-208 mutant cells.
source: Remarkably, RT-qPCR of four reporter RNAs revealed a similar increase in mis6-302 cells as in cut14-208 mutant cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Chromosome missegregation during mitosis resulting from condensin inactivation can lead to gene deregulation.
source: This argues that chromosome missegregation during mitosis, which results from condensin inactivation, can lead to gene deregulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with mis6-302 and other mutants.

claim: The expression of six different families of tRNAs is modestly increased in cut3-477 condensin mutant cells grown at 36°C.
source: It has been reported that the expression of six different families of tRNAs, as measured by RT-PCR, is modestly increased in cut3-477 condensin mutant cells grown at the restrictive temperature of 36°C (Iwasaki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claim: A clear increase in tRNA levels was observed in cut3-m26, cut14-90, and cut14-208 cells.
source: Although we could not detect any significant change in tRNA levels in cut3-477 cells, we observed a clear increase in cut3-m26, cut14-90 and cut14-208 cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The increase in tRNA levels correlated with the frequency of chromosome missegregation and with the accumulation of mRNAs and ncRNAs.
source: The increase correlated with the frequency of chromosome missegregation and with the accumulation of mRNAs and ncRNAs (compare with Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis of RT-qPCR and cytological data.

claim: Preventing aneuploidy in cut14-208 mutant cells by cdc15-140 restored normal steady state levels of tRNAs.
source: Importantly, preventing aneuploidy in cut14-208 mutant cells by using the cdc15-140 mutation restored a normal steady state level of these tRNAs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Non-condensin mutations that disrupted chromosome segregation (ptr4-1, cut9-665, mis6-302) resulted in increased tRNA levels similar to cut14-208.
source: Conversely, non-condensin mutations that disrupted chromosome segregation, such as ptr4-1, cut9-665 or mis6-302, resulted in a similar increase in tRNA levels as in cut14-208 (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: The effects of ptr4-1 and cut9-665 on tRNA levels were more comparable to cut14-208 than to mis6-302.
source: We noticed, however, that the effects of ptr4-1 and cut9-665 were more comparable to the cut14-208 mutation than to the mis6-302 mutation, which did not upregulate the tRNAs SER +MET and THR (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an observation from RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The difference in tRNA upregulation between cut14-208 and mis6-302 is unlikely to be caused by DNA damage.
source: This difference between cut14-208 and mis6-302 is unlikely to be caused by DNA damage that occurs in cut14-208 cells upon mitotic exit, as neither Camptothecin nor Zeocin treatment increased tRNA levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from DNA damage experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The difference in tRNA upregulation might be a manifestation of phenotypic variability associated with the aneuploid condition.
source: It might rather be the manifestation of an inherent phenotypic variability associated with the aneuploid condition (Beach et al., 2017) (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation.

claim: The imbalance in genomic content from chromosome missegregation during mitosis is a major cause of deregulation of cellular RNAs when condensin is impaired.
source: Nevertheless, taken together, these results strongly suggest that the imbalance in genomic content that results from chromosome missegregation during mitosis is a major cause of the deregulation of most, if not all, cellular RNAs when the function of condensin is impaired.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments with different mutants.

claim: Condensin plays a major role in the segregation of the rDNA during late anaphase in budding yeast.
source: It had been reported that condensin plays a major role in the segregation of the rDNA during late anaphase in budding yeast (Freeman et al., 2000; Sullivan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citations.

claim: Condensin plays a major role in the segregation of the rDNA during late anaphase in fission yeast.
source: We reached the same conclusion in fission yeast, confirming previous observations (Nakazawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study confirming prior research.

claim: Sister rDNA copies failed to separate during anaphase in cut14-208 mutant cells, frequently resulting in anucleolate daughter cells.
source: When we scored the segregation of a GFP-labelled version of the rDNA-binding protein Gar2, we found that sister rDNA copies failed to separate during anaphase in cut14-208 mutant cells, frequently resulting in the formation of anucleolate daughter cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The ptr4-1 and mis6-302 mutants also exhibited a high rate of anucleolate cell formation.
source: The ptr4-1 and mis6-302 mutants also exhibited a high rate of anucleolate cell formation (Figure 7A), whereas the cdc15-140 mutation suppressed the formation of anucleolate cells in the cut14-208 mutant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The cdc15-140 mutation suppressed the formation of anucleolate cells in the cut14-208 mutant.
source: The ptr4-1 and mis6-302 mutants also exhibited a high rate of anucleolate cell formation (Figure 7A), whereas the cdc15-140 mutation suppressed the formation of anucleolate cells in the cut14-208 mutant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The inability to properly segregate the rDNA during anaphase correlates with the accumulation of mRNAs and ncRNAs targeted by the RNA-exosome.
source: Thus, the inability to properly segregate the rDNA during anaphase correlates with the accumulation of mRNAs and ncRNAs targeted by the RNA-exosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from correlation of rDNA segregation and RNA accumulation data.

claim: Rrp6 is enriched in the nucleolus and its amount was markedly reduced in cut14-208 anucleolate daughter cells.
source: Co-immunostaining of Rrp6 tagged with a myc epitope and Gar2 tagged with GFP confirmed the nuclear localisation of Rrp6 and its marked enrichment within the nucleolus (Figure 7B). In a wild-type background, Rrp6 appeared evenly distributed between nuclei in post-mitotic daughter cells (median signal ratio ~1). In sharp contrast, the amount of Rrp6 was markedly reduced in cut14-208 anucleolate daughter cells compared to their nucleolate counterparts (median signal ratio ~0.25; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A similar asymmetric distribution of Dis3 was observed in post-mitotic cut14-208 cells.
source: We observed a similar asymmetric distribution of Dis3 tagged with an HA epitope in post-mitotic cut14-208 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Residual levels of Rrp6 and Dis3 proteins remained detectable in anucleolate cells.
source: Residual levels of Rrp6 and Dis3 proteins remained detectable in anucleolate cells (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), which suggests that a small fraction of Rrp6 and Dis3 molecules is transmitted to daughter cells independently of the rDNA.
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A small fraction of Rrp6 and Dis3 molecules is transmitted to daughter cells independently of the rDNA.
source: Residual levels of Rrp6 and Dis3 proteins remained detectable in anucleolate cells (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), which suggests that a small fraction of Rrp6 and Dis3 molecules is transmitted to daughter cells independently of the rDNA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from immunofluorescence data.

claim: Rrp6 accumulates predominantly on chromosomes during mitosis in Drosophila.
source: Knowing that Rrp6 accumulates predominantly on chromosomes during mitosis in Drosophila (Graham et al., 2009), we propose that the bulk of Rrp6 and Dis3 might similarly co-segregate with the nucleolus in fission yeast, while a fraction is presumably transmitted to daughter cells in association with chromatin or within the nucleoplasm.
evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claim: The bulk of Rrp6 and Dis3 might co-segregate with the nucleolus in fission yeast, while a fraction is transmitted to daughter cells in association with chromatin or within the nucleoplasm.
source: Knowing that Rrp6 accumulates predominantly on chromosomes during mitosis in Drosophila (Graham et al., 2009), we propose that the bulk of Rrp6 and Dis3 might similarly co-segregate with the nucleolus in fission yeast, while a fraction is presumably transmitted to daughter cells in association with chromatin or within the nucleoplasm.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on prior research and current findings.

claim: The segregation of Dis3-mNeonGreen into daughter cells was severely impaired during the first cell division after condensin inactivation by Brn1 cleavage in budding yeast.
source: Live cell imaging in budding yeast furthermore demonstrated that the segregation into the daughter cells of a mNeonGreen-tagged version of Dis3 was severely impaired during the first cell division after condensin inactivation by Brn1 cleavage (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from live cell imaging shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Condensin deficiency leads to rDNA non-disjunction during anaphase and production of anucleolate post-mitotic cells depleted of Rrp6 and Dis3.
source: We conclude that condensin deficiency leads to rDNA non-disjunction during anaphase and the production of anucleolate post-mitotic cells, which are depleted of Rrp6 and Dis3.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings.

claim: mug93as levels were considerably higher in cut14-208 mutant cells than in wild-type cells.
source: Single molecule RNA-FISH showed that the ncRNA mug93as produced very faint signals in wild-type cells (Figure 7D), consistent with its active degradation by the RNA-exosome (Figure 1D). On the contrary, mug93as levels were considerably higher in cut14-208 mutant cells (Figure 7D), which confirms our previous RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data.
evidence: This is a finding from single molecule RNA-FISH shown in Figure 7D.

claim: mug93as RNA accumulated mainly in anucleolate cells devoid of Gar2-GFP, with highest signals in anucleolate cells with low chromatin amount.
source: Crucially, mug93as RNA accumulated mainly in anucleolate cells devoid of Gar2-GFP, with the highest signals in anucleolate cells with low chromatin amount, as judged by DAPI staining.
evidence: This is a finding from single molecule RNA-FISH analysis.

claim: A control mRNA (cct2) was evenly distributed between daughter cells in the cut14-208 mutant.
source: In sharp contrast, a control mRNA (cct2) was evenly distributed between the daughter cells in the cut14-208 mutant (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a finding from single molecule RNA-FISH shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Condensin loss-of-function leads to formation of anucleolate cells that accumulate RNA-exosome-sensitive transcripts.
source: We conclude that condensin loss-of-function leads to the formation of anucleolate cells that accumulate RNA-exosome-sensitive transcripts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from single molecule RNA-FISH and other data.

claim: The functional integrity of condensin is dispensable for the maintenance of proper gene expression during interphase and mitosis in fission and budding yeasts.
source: Here, we challenge the idea that condensin complexes directly regulate transcription by providing compelling evidence that the functional integrity of condensin is dispensable for the maintenance of proper gene expression during interphase and even mitosis in fission and budding yeasts.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental findings.

claim: Condensin deficiency alters the transcriptome of post-mitotic cells in fission yeast, but this effect is mostly the indirect consequence of chromosome missegregation during anaphase.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we show that condensin deficiency alters the transcriptome of post-mitotic cells in fission yeast. However, this effect is mostly, if not entirely, the indirect consequence of chromosome missegregation during anaphase.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental findings.

claim: Condensin plays no direct role in the control of gene expression in fission and budding yeasts, but is essential for maintaining proper gene expression by contributing to accurate chromosome segregation during mitosis.
source: Our findings therefore indicate that condensin plays no direct role in the control of gene expression in fission and budding yeasts, but is essential for the maintenance of proper gene expression by contributing to the accurate segregation of chromosomes during mitosis.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental findings.

claim: cut14-208 condensin mutant cells accumulate tRNAs, mRNAs, ncRNAs and 3'-extended read-through transcripts.
source: Strand-specific RNA-seq and RT-qPCR analyses reveal that cut14-208 condensin mutant cells accumulate tRNAs, mRNAs, ncRNAs and 3'-extended read-through transcripts.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from RNA-seq and RT-qPCR analyses.

claim: Other condensin mutants (cut3-m26, cut14-90, cut14-180) exhibit similar increases in RNA levels as cut14-208.
source: Other condensin mutants such as cut3-m26, cut14-90 and cut14-180 exhibit similar increases in RNA levels, arguing that condensin takes part in proper gene expression in fission yeast, similar to other organisms.
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis of multiple condensin mutants.

claim: When cut14-208 cells were synchronised at S, G2 phase, or metaphase, RNA levels remained unchanged.
source: However, when cut14-208 cells were synchronised at S or G2 phase or even at metaphase, RNA levels remained unchanged.
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis of synchronized cells.

claim: The suppressive effect of cdc15-140 upon cut14-208 on changes in gene expression argues that condensin impinges on gene expression in a cytokinesis-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, the prevalent suppressive effect of cdc15-140 upon cut14-208 on changes in gene expression argues that condensin impinges on gene expression in a cytokinesis-dependent manner, and therefore in an indirect manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with cdc15-140 cut14-208 double mutant.

claim: Condensin deficiency makes no predominant impact on the steady state level of RNAs in post-mitotic cells by itself.
source: Importantly, it also implies that condensin deficiency makes by itself no predominant impact on the steady state level of RNAs in post-mitotic cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the suppressive effect of cdc15-140.

claim: Condensin plays no major direct role in the maintenance of proper gene expression during interphase or mitosis in fission yeast.
source: Thus, although we cannot rule out the possibility that subtle impacts of condensin on the dynamics of transcription might have escaped our detection, our data strongly indicate that condensin plays no major direct role in the maintenance of proper gene expression during interphase or during mitosis in fission yeast.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple synchronization and genetic experiments.

claim: Condensin is largely dispensable for the maintenance of gene expression programs during G1 phase or metaphase in budding yeast.
source: Concordantly, we show that also in budding yeast, condensin is largely dispensable for the maintenance of gene expression programs during the G1 phase or during metaphase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from tiling array experiments in budding yeast.

claim: The separation of budding and fission yeast lineages is thought to have occurred ~420 million years ago.
source: Note that the separation of the budding and fission yeast lineages is thought to have occurred ~420 million years ago, which makes them as distant from each other as either is from animals (Sipiczki, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast evolution supported by citation.

claim: In two evolutionarily distant organisms (budding and fission yeast), condensin complexes play no major direct role in the maintenance of an established gene expression program.
source: Thus, in two evolutionarily distant organisms, condensin complexes play no major direct role in the maintenance of an established gene expression program.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments in both yeast species.

claim: The increased RNA levels in fission yeast cells defective for condensin are the indirect consequence of a failure during late mitosis caused by lack of condensin activity.
source: The corollary is that the increased RNA levels exhibited by fission yeast cells defective for condensin must be the indirect consequence of a failure during late mitosis caused by a lack of condensin activity.
evidence: This is a logical inference drawn from the finding that condensin has no direct role in gene expression.

claim: Suppressing the production of genetically unbalanced daughter cells by cdc15-140 is sufficient to restore an almost normal transcriptome despite condensin being impaired.
source: Furthermore, suppressing the production of genetically unbalanced daughter cells by the cytokinesis mutation cdc15-140 is sufficient to restore an almost normal transcriptome, despite condensin being impaired by the cut14-208 mutation.
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis of cdc15-140 cut14-208 double mutant.

claim: Preventing proper chromosome segregation by mutations in separase, APC/C, or kinetochore is sufficient to trigger accumulation of aberrant transcripts like in cut14-208 cells.
source: Reciprocally, preventing proper chromosome segregation by mutations in separase (ptr4-1), the APC/C (cut9-665) or the kinetochore (mis6-302) is sufficient to trigger the accumulation of aberrant transcripts alike in cut14-208 cells.
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis of multiple mutants.

claim: The missegregation of chromosomes during anaphase is the principal mechanism responsible for changes in RNA levels in condensin mutant cells.
source: Therefore, the missegregation of chromosomes during anaphase appears to be the principal responsible mechanism for the changes in RNA levels exhibited by condensin mutant cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple genetic experiments.

claim: Sister-rDNAs systematically fail to disjoin during anaphase in cut14-208 condensin mutant cells, leading to production of anucleolate daughter cells.
