source: Indeed, we show (1) that sister-rDNAs systematically fail to disjoin during anaphase in cut14-208 condensin mutant cells, leading to the production of anucleolate daughter cells;
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis.

claim: Rrp6 and Dis3, which are enriched in the nucleolus, become depleted from anucleolate cut14-208 cells.
source: (2) Rrp6 and Dis3, which are enriched in the nucleolus, become depleted from anucleolate cut14-208 cells;
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence analysis.

claim: The reduction of Rrp6 and Dis3 from anucleolate condensin mutant cells coincides with increased steady state levels of RNA-exosome-sensitive transcripts.
source: (3) the reduction of Rrp6 and Dis3 from anucleolate condensin mutant cells coincides with an increased steady state level of RNA-exosome-sensitive transcripts;
evidence: This is a correlation observed from immunofluorescence and RNA-seq data.

claim: The antisense RNA mug93as accumulates principally if not exclusively in anucleolate condensin mutant cells.
source: and (4) an RNA-exosome sensitive transcript, the antisense RNA mug93as, accumulates principally if not exclusively in anucleolate condensin mutant cells, as expected from an impaired degradation.
evidence: This is a finding from single molecule RNA-FISH analysis.

claim: Rrp6 accumulates predominantly on chromosomes during mitosis in Drosophila.
source: Knowing that Rrp6 accumulates predominantly on chromosomes during mitosis in Drosophila (Graham et al., 2009), we propose that the bulk of Rrp6 and Dis3 might similarly co-segregate with the nucleolus in fission yeast, while a fraction is presumably transmitted to daughter cells in association with chromatin or within the nucleoplasm.
evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claim: The co-depletion of Rrp6 and Dis3 from anucleolate cut14-208 cells explains why the transcriptomes of cut14-208 and rrp6Δ strains overlap only partially.
source: The co-depletion of Rrp6 and Dis3 from anucleolate cut14-208 cells provides a straightforward explanation as to why the transcriptomes of the cut14-208 and rrp6Δ strains overlap only partially, and to the slight additive effect exhibited by the cut14-208 and rrp6Δ mutations with respect to the accumulation of mug93as (Figure 1D) and of 3'-extented hsp9 RNA (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an explanation inferred from the co-depletion of both RNA-exosome components.

claim: Condensin deficiency impairs chromosome segregation during anaphase, leading to chromatin bridges and rDNA non-disjunction.
source: Condensin deficiency impairs chromosome segregation during anaphase, and notably leads to chromatin bridges and the non-disjunction of the rDNA.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cytological analysis.

claim: Upon mitotic exit, failure to properly segregate chromosomes alters the karyotype of daughter cells and creates an aneuploid condition that changes cellular RNA content.
source: Upon mitotic exit, this failure to properly segregate chromosomes alters the karyotype of daughter cells and creates an aneuploid condition that changes the cellular RNA content.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from FACScan and RNA-seq data.

claim: Rrp6 and Dis3 enriched in the nucleolus during mitosis become depleted from anucleolate daughter cells, reducing RNA-exosome activity.
source: In particular, Rrp6 and Dis3 which are enriched in the nucleolus during mitosis become depleted from anucleolate daughter cells. This reduces the activity of the RNA-exosome, allowing the accumulation of RNA molecules that are normally actively degraded by the RNA-exosome, such as ncRNAs and 3'-extended RNAs.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation drawn from immunofluorescence and RNA-seq data.

claim: Chromosome missegregation caused by condensin deficiency indirectly changes cellular RNA contents in fission yeast.
source: This sequence of events illustrate how chromosome missegregation caused by condensin deficiency indirectly changes cellular RNA contents in fission yeast.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the mechanistic model.

claim: Aneuploid cells exhibit gene-specific deregulations along a stereotypical 'aneuploid stress-response'.
source: Aneuploid cells exhibit gene-specific deregulations along a more stereotypical 'aneuploid stress-response' characterised by an increased expression of genes involved in the response to stress and a down-regulation of cell-cycle and proliferation genes (Santaguida and Amon, 2015; Sheltzer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about aneuploidy supported by citations.

claim: Premalignant murine T-cells defective for condensin II exhibit a transcriptome evocative of a stress response to aneuploidy.
source: Premalignant murine T-cells defective for condensin II exhibit a transcriptome evocative of a stress response to aneuploidy (Woodward et al., 2016).
evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claim: Depletion of Smc2 in a human neuroblastoma cell line modifies expression of genes mainly involved in cell cycle progression or DNA damage response.
source: Similarly, the depletion of Smc2, and hence the reduction of both condensin I and II, in a human neuroblastoma cell line modifies the expression of a large number of genes implicated mainly in cell cycle progression or DNA damage response (Murakami-Tonami et al., 2014).
evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claim: No clear transcriptomic signature of aneuploidy stress response was observed in cut14-208 mutant cells.
source: However, we did not observed such a clear transcriptomic signature in cut14-208 mutant cells.
evidence: This is an observation from RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Condensin deficiency causes mostly severing of chromosome arms by the cytokinetic ring in fission yeast, leading to partial- or micro-aneuploidy.
source: One possible explanation is that condensin deficiency causes mostly the severing of chromosome arms by the cytokinetic ring in fission yeast, which presumably leads to the gain or loss of chromosomal fragments rather than of entire chromosomes. The resulting partial- or micro-aneuploidy (Pfau and Amon, 2012) might, in contrast to a whole chromosomal aneuploidy, not elicit a robust aneuploidy stress response, which presumably stems from the concomitant change in number of many genes that have little impact when varied individually (Santaguida and Amon, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of aneuploidy stress response signature, supported by citations.

claim: Different types of aneuploidy might have varying impacts on the transcriptome.
source: That different types of aneuploidy might have varying impacts on the transcriptome might also explain the slight differences we observed between the tRNA contents of cut14-208 and mis6-302 mutant cells, which missegregate entire chromosomes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed differences between mutants.

claim: Multiple mechanisms linked to chromosome instability and aberrant karyotypes likely concur to modify the transcriptome when condensin is defective.
source: In any cases, multiple mechanisms linked to chromosome instability and the genesis of aberrant karyotypes most likely concur to modify the transcriptome when condensin is defective.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the complexity of mechanisms involved.

claim: The slight up-regulation of histone genes in cut14-208 mutant cells has been attributed to indirect stabilization of the transcription factor Ams2 during defective anaphase.
source: For instance, the slight up-regulation of histone genes that we observed in cut14-208 mutant cells has previously been attributed to an indirect stabilization of the transcription factor Ams2 during defective anaphase (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claim: Cohesin accumulates at intergenic regions flanked by co-transcribed convergent genes where it prevents transcription beyond canonical termination sites.
source: Probably pushed by active RNA Pol II, cohesin accumulates at intergenic regions that are flanked by co-transcribed convergent genes, where it prevents transcription to proceed beyond canonical termination sites (Gullerova and Proudfoot, 2008).
evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claim: In the case of unidirectional transcription, read-through RNAs are produced in a cohesin-independent manner.
source: It is important to note that in the case of unidirectional transcription, read-through RNAs are produced in a cohesin–independent manner (Gullerova and Proudfoot, 2008), implying that cohesin plays the role of a roadblock for RNA polymerases specifically at the 3'ends of co-transcribed convergent genes.
evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claim: Cohesin remains bound to chromatin in cut14-208 cells, including at convergent genes that exhibit read-through transcripts.
source: Our observation that cohesin remains bound to chromatin in cut14-208 cells, including at convergent genes that exhibit read-through transcripts, plus the lack of any noticeable increase in Pol II occupancy, argue that condensin is unlikely to prevent read-thought transcripts through a same mechanism.
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP experiments.

claim: 43% of read-through RNAs originate from genes oriented in tandem in cut14-208 cells.
source: The fact that 43% of read-through RNAs originate from genes oriented in tandem in cut14-208 cells further support this conclusion.
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Besides cohesin-dependent termination, another pathway dependent upon condensin exists that prevents read-through transcripts.
source: Thus, besides cohesin-dependent termination, another pathway dependent upon condensin must also exist that prevents read-through transcripts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data on read-through transcripts.

claim: Condensin is unlikely to play a direct role in preventing read-through transcripts, since cdc15-140 cut14-208 double mutant cells no longer accumulate read-through RNAs.
source: However, and crucially, condensin is unlikely to play a direct role in this second pathway, since cdc15-140 cut14-208 double mutant cells no longer accumulate read-through RNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from RNA-seq data of double mutant cells.

claim: The lack of read-through RNAs in cdc15-140 cut14-208 cells suggests condensin is unlikely to exert any major roadblock effect on active RNA polymerases.
source: Furthermore, given that cut14-208 reduces the binding of condensin to chromatin (Nakazawa et al., 2015), the lack of read-through RNAs in cdc15-140 cut14-208 cells suggests that condensin is unlikely to exert any major roadblock effect on active RNA polymerases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from RNA-seq data and prior research on condensin binding.

claim: The overlap between cut14-208 and rrp6Δ cells suggests it is the degradation of read-through transcripts that is impaired.
source: The overlap between cut14-208 and rrp6Δ cells suggests instead that it is the degradation of read-through transcripts that is impaired.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overlap analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Read-through transcripts are produced in wild-type cells.
source: Read-through transcripts are produced in wild-type cells (Gullerova and Proudfoot, 2008; Zofall et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Read-through RNAs are naturally produced at both tandem and convergent genes in wild-type cells but are rapidly degraded by Rrp6.
source: We therefore propose that read-through RNAs are naturally produced both at tandem and convergent genes in wild-type cells, but are rapidly degraded by Rrp6.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: Chromosome missegregation during mitosis caused by condensin deficiency induces accumulation of read-through transcripts by depleting Rrp6 from karyotypically abnormal daughter cells.
source: Chromosome missegregation during mitosis caused by condensin deficiency induces their accumulation, despite the presence of cohesin, at least in part by depleting Rrp6 from karyotypically abnormal daughter cells.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data.

claim: Sister-rDNA almost systematically non-disjoin during anaphase in fission yeast condensin mutant cells.
source: Our finding that sister-rDNA almost systematically non-disjoin during anaphase in fission yeast condensin mutant cells is consistent with the severe missegregation of the rDNA observed in budding yeast and human cells deprived of functional condensin complexes (D'Ambrosio et al., 2008b; Freeman et al., 2000; Samoshkin et al., 2012), and with the idea that decatenation of sister-rDNA during late anaphase relies upon condensin (D'Ambrosio et al., 2008a ).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study consistent with prior research.

claim: The asymmetric partitioning of Dis3 in budding yeast daughter cells after condensin inactivation can be interpreted as a consequence of failure to disjoin sister-rDNA during anaphase.
source: In that context, the asymmetric partitioning of the ribonuclease Dis3 that we observed in budding yeast daughter cells after the inactivation of condensin by TEV cleavage can be reasonably interpreted as a consequence of a failure to disjoin sister-rDNA during anaphase.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the live imaging data in budding yeast.

claim: Mutations affecting condensin generate anucleolate cells that accumulate polyadenylated RNAs in budding yeast.
source: In addition, it has been reported that mutations affecting condensin generate anucleolate cells that accumulate polyadenylated RNAs in budding yeast (Paul and Montpetit, 2016).
evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claim: The missegregation of the rDNA that occurs when condensin is impaired presumably impinges upon gene expression in budding yeast, like in fission yeast.
source: Therefore, the missegregation of the rDNA that frequently occurs during anaphase when condensin is impaired presumably impinges upon gene expression in budding yeast, alike in fission yeast.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from findings in both yeast species.

claim: Chromatin bridges are almost systematically severed by the cytokinetic ring in cut14-208 mutant cells, while severing of the nucleolus is extremely infrequent.
source: One related aspect that remains puzzling, however, is that chromatin bridges are almost systematically severed by the cytokinetic ring in cut14-208 mutant cells, while the severing of the nucleolus is extremely infrequent (<10% of the cases).
evidence: This is an observation from cytological analysis.

claim: The persistence of the nucleolus in the axis of cleavage might mechanically hinder cytokinesis or trigger a wait signal.
source: The persistence of the nucleolus in the axis of cleavage might mechanically hinder cytokinesis, or trigger a wait signal.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation.

claim: Condensin deficiency might cause DNA double-strand breaks at fragile sites located on the centromere-proximal border of the rDNA cluster.
source: Alternatively, condensin deficiency might cause DNA double-strand breaks at fragile sites located on the centromere-proximal border of the cluster of rDNA repeats, allowing the displacement of untangled sister-rDNA towards one pole of the mitotic spindle through a spring-relaxation effect.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation.

claim: A focused role for condensin in organising a region proximal to the rDNA, located on its centromeric side, has been reported in budding yeast.
source: A focused role for condensin in organising a region proximal to the rDNA, and located on its centromeric side, has been reported in budding yeast (Schalbetter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claim: In HeLa cells, depletion of SMC2 induces DNA breaks predominantly in repetitive DNA, including the rDNA/Nucleolar Organising Regions.
source: In HeLa cells, the depletion of SMC2 induces DNA breaks predominantly in repetitive DNA, including the rDNA/Nucleolar Organising Regions (Samoshkin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claim: Missegregation of the rDNA in budding and fission yeast when condensin is impaired might reveal an evolutionarily-conserved acute dependency of repeated DNA elements upon condensin.
source: Thus, missegregation of the rDNA in budding and fission yeast cells when condensin is impaired might reveal an evolutionarily-conserved acute dependency of repeated DNA elements upon condensin for their segregation and integrity.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from findings across species.

claim: Condensin loss of function might have similar confounding impacts on the preservation of structural integrity and proper expression of tandem repetitive DNA arrays in mammalian genomes.
source: Given the prevalence of tandem repetitive DNA arrays in mammalian genomes (Warburton et al., 2008), it is tempting to speculate that condensin loss of function might have similar confounding impacts on the preservation of their structural integrity and proper expression.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation to mammalian systems supported by citation.

claim: The three-dimensional organisation of the genome influences gene expression.
source: Studies performed over the past 20 years have shown that the three-dimensional organisation of the genome influences gene expression, raising the key question of the role played by SMC complexes in the control of gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.

claim: There are robust examples of cohesin-mediated regulation of cell-type-specific gene expression.
source: Although there are robust examples of cohesin-mediated regulation of cell-type-specific gene expression (Merkenschlager and Nora, 2016), for instance through enhancer-to-promoter interactions (Ing-Simmons et al., 2015; Kagey et al., 2010), a recent study has raised the idea that the involvement of cohesin in the maintenance of an established gene expression program might be less prominent than initially thought (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of prior research findings supported by citations.

claim: The involvement of cohesin in the maintenance of an established gene expression program might be less prominent than initially thought.
source: Although there are robust examples of cohesin-mediated regulation of cell-type-specific gene expression (Merkenschlager and Nora, 2016), for instance through enhancer-to-promoter interactions (Ing-Simmons et al., 2015; Kagey et al., 2010), a recent study has raised the idea that the involvement of cohesin in the maintenance of an established gene expression program might be less prominent than initially thought (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a recent finding from prior research supported by citation.

claim: There has been no clear case where the influence of condensin I or II on gene expression has been dissociated from a possible confounding effect of chromosome missegregation.
source: Similarly, despite ample reports of cells defective for condensin I or II exhibiting changes in gene expression (Bhalla et al., 2002; Dowen et al., 2013; He et al., 2016; Iwasaki et al., 2010; Kranz et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015; Longworth et al., 2012; Lupo et al., 2001; Murakami-Tonami et al., 2014; Rawlings et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2016; Yuen et al., 2017), to the best of our knowledge, there has thus far been no clear case where the influence of condensin I or II on gene expression has been dissociated from a possible confounding effect of chromosome missegregation.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the prior literature.

claim: This work challenges the concept of gene regulation as a collective property of SMC complexes.
source: By providing evidence that condensin plays no major direct role in the control of gene expression in fission and budding yeasts, and showing that condensin impinges on gene expression by preserving the stability of the genome during mitosis, our work challenges the concept of gene regulation as a collective property of SMC complexes, and should help to better define future studies on the role of canonical condensins in gene expression in other organisms.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the implications of the study.
